1:
The chapter opens with a change of ground rather than a change of question. Having failed to find the felicity of man in study, Solomon adjourns, as Matthew Henry puts it, out of his library and council-chamber into the park and the playhouse, exchanging philosophers and grave senators for the wits and gallants of his court. The trial Henry describes is a specific one: whether a man could be happy if he kept himself and his company always in a merry humour, furnished with every ingenious turn and repartee he could invent or pick up. Henry calls the move a great step downward, from the noble pleasures of the intellect to the brutal ones of sense, but grants that a thorough trial must knock at this door, since a great part of mankind imagine they have already found there what he was in quest of. John Gill and John Wesley both read the move as deliberate: disappointed of his hopes from knowledge, he resolved to try another course. Adam Clarke supplies a verse paraphrase in which appetite whispers the invitation to turn back from the rugged thorny road of wisdom which so ill repays the toil, and enter pleasure's flowery paths. Charles Ellicott notes that the address is literally to his heart, and that the word rendered enjoy is in Hebrew see.

The verdict on laughter falls at once, and the commentators divide over how wide it reaches. Gill holds that the faculty of laughter is given for a use, and that moderate laughter serves the health of the body and the pleasure of the mind; it is the laughter poured out on every trivial occasion and indulged to excess that makes a man look like a madman, and that ends in heaviness. He offers a second rendering in which the words are spoken not about laughter but to it: thou art mad, and I will shun thee as one shuns a madman. Henry says the same of mirth, which soberly and seasonably used is a good thing, fitting a man for business and softening the toils of life. Clarke narrows the target further, to intemperate pleasure rather than any sober enjoyment of the world. Keil and Delitzsch will not soften it: the participle is one of raving madness, and the man addressed is like someone who finds his pleasure in self-destruction. Clarke reads the two clauses as a small piece of stagecraft, laughter and mirth personified as two women, the first told to her face that she is mad, the second thought so far beneath notice that he only points at her and turns his back. Wesley ends the verse by challenging all the Epicures in the world to give a solid answer to it.

The third verse describes a more careful experiment, and the disagreement is over how much of it wisdom actually governs. Gill insists the wine is not intoxication but good living generally, food and drink of the best, taken in a liberal but innocently cheerful way. Clarke says plainly that where he had earlier thrown off all restraint he now took the middle course. Ellicott makes the grammar carry the point: the word rendered acquainting is properly guiding, and is used of the man who drives an animal or the shepherd who leads a flock, so that what is contemplated is an enjoyment controlled by prudence rather than an unrestrained one. Delitzsch agrees that the heart kept the direction by means of wisdom, and adds that the verb translated sought means to spy out, the same word used of searching out a resting place. Wesley alone puts it as a mixture, wine and wisdom together, tried to see whether satisfaction could be reached that way. Ellicott closes on the phrase for their span of life, which he takes as the numbered and therefore few days a man has to spend on the question.
4:
The catalogue of works is read as the second and larger half of the same experiment. John Gill is careful that these were not trifles — he sets Solomon against the emperor who spent his hours catching flies — but works becoming the grandeur of his state. Adam Clarke fills in the buildings: palace after palace, the house of the forest of Lebanon, a house for the queen, the temple. Keil and Delitzsch supply the setting rather than the list, and give the fullest historical frame here. A love of wisdom, a sense of the beautiful in nature and art, and a striving after splendour were fundamental in Solomon; his reign was a period of undisturbed peace; he was the man of rest, and the commonwealth stood at a pinnacle of worldly glory till then unattained, with the attendant danger of being lost in the world.

Two of the terms draw comment out of proportion to their length. The word behind orchards is the one Clarke doubts is native Hebrew at all, pointing to the Persian and Arabic word for a pleasant garden from which our paradise descends; Charles Ellicott agrees on the Persian origin and prefers to render it parks, adding that trees giving shade as well as fruit were an almost necessary part of kingly luxury under an Eastern sun. Gill, who takes Solomon's botanical learning seriously, assumes a herbal garden stocked with everything curious and useful. On the pools, Gill and Ellicott point to the three great reservoirs cut in the rock south of Bethlehem, each lower than the last so that water passes from one to the next, still called the Pools of Solomon and probably the place Josephus names in describing his luxury; Ellicott notes the necessity of tanks in a land whose few streams dry in summer. John Wesley reads the wood they water as nurseries of young trees, so many as to make a forest.

At the end of the eighth verse the text becomes genuinely dark, and the commentators divide. Two Hebrew words stand where our version reads musical instruments of all sorts, and Clarke says flatly that they are acknowledged on all hands to be inexplicable. He lists the attempts — male and female captives, cups and flagons, cooks and confectioners, a species of musical composition traced to a Phoenician woman named Sido — and settles, with more probability, on wives and concubines, since these are otherwise unmentioned while music has already been named. Ellicott reaches the same place: the guesses are too numerous to recount, the rendering of our version is by no means among the most probable, and concubines is most in favour, though commentators differ over how to justify it. Delitzsch simply renders the pair as mistress and mistresses. Clarke reduces the rest of the verse to a sober list: taxes levied and tribute given, which together make the peculiar treasure of kings.

The claim that wisdom remained with him is read two ways. Delitzsch and Gill take it at face value, as the word of a man who kept his judgment through the trial and observed decorum in it, so that the verdict at the end is competent. Wesley reads it as a limited admission — that he was not yet wholly seduced from God — which concedes what the histories elsewhere report of Solomon's later years. Gill notes that he now sits down for the first time and considers what all this cost in expense and toil of mind, and that he is qualified as few men to give a just estimate. Delitzsch says of the answer that nothing remained of the enjoyment but the feeling of emptiness; Clarke that it promised the good he wished for and could not perform the promise, leaving the soul discontented; Wesley that the pleasure was past and he was never the better for it, as empty as before.
12:
Having exhausted pleasure, the search returns to where it began. Matthew Henry pictures a man sick of his pleasures and nauseating them, turning back to speculation for a second hearing of a case he had already tried; if the verdict is the same on rehearing, the judgment is decisive. John Gill and John Wesley agree that the return is a fresh trial rather than a repetition, undertaken to see whether something had been overlooked. The question that follows is read two ways, and Charles Ellicott sets out both. Our version yields the good sense that if the king has failed in his experiment there is little likelihood a private man will do better, and Henry, Adam Clarke and Wesley all take it so: no one can expect to find more in the world than Solomon did, since none ever had such means of gratification, and the baffled trial need not be repeated. Ellicott himself prefers the simpler reading, that the phrase means the king's successor, as it does later in the book, and that the successor can only run the same round already trodden — which fits the theme of the whole section, that in human affairs there is no progress. Keil and Delitzsch spend the verse instead on rejecting two proposed renderings, Mendelssohn's and Hitzig's, on the ground that the two connecting particles are copulative and not correlative.

What follows is a concession, and all the voices treat it as one. Wisdom has the advantage of folly as light has the advantage of darkness. Gill grants that natural wisdom, though it holds no true happiness, greatly exceeds folly; Wesley allows thus much, that wisdom is of far greater use than vain pleasures. Delitzsch observes that the word which until now has meant actual result and enduring gain here means only preference, and Ellicott notes the same word rendered profit. On the wise man's eyes, Wesley reads simply that they are in their proper place, so that he foresees and avoids many mischiefs; Gill adds a second and spiritual sense in which the head is Christ and the eyes of the wise are on him alone. Clarke gives the contrast as verse, the wise weighing the consequence of what they undertake, the fool groping in darkness or running a race with heedless steps on the brink of a precipice. Delitzsch puts it that the fool is blind although he has eyes, and so has as good as none.

The concession is withdrawn in the same breath by the one event that falls to both. Clarke notes the emphatic repetition in the Hebrew, the event happening to me, even me, and draws the warning that wisdom is equally subject to the common accidents of life and so cannot make us completely happy. Wesley says the same more plainly: both come at last to one end, and death takes away all difference between them. Whether the loss of remembrance that follows is absolute is disputed. Gill holds it is not, and reads the saying as spoken of natural wisdom only. A wise man may be remembered a while, and then a brighter genius rises, or is thought to, and outshines him, and his writings are neglected and buried; but those who are truly good and wise are held in everlasting remembrance. Clarke takes the words as they stand, time sweeping away all remembrance save the few out of millions preserved for a while in the page of history, and Wesley points to the wise men of former ages whose very names and monuments are lost. Ellicott raises a question none of the others touch, arguing that the thought suits Solomon reflecting on himself but not a later writer who had chosen Solomon as his hero, and concluding that what is recorded here is the history of Solomon's reflections rather than the book's final conclusions.
17:
Matthew Henry treats the turn here as a third experiment rather than a conclusion to the second: after a contemplative life and a voluptuous life, Solomon betook himself to an active one. Business, Henry says, is a thing wise men take pleasure in — they are in their element when they are in it and complain when they are out of it — so this is where the good a man should do might reasonably be found. What defeats it is the qualifier. The labour is under the sun, and Henry sets against it a business above the sun which is perpetual blessedness, work done in conformity to God's will as it is done in heaven, which no man has reason to hate or to despair of. He is also careful that the labour Solomon hated was the better sort, not the drudgery of the hewers of wood and drawers of water, but rational business carried on in wisdom and knowledge and equity, relating to the government of a kingdom.

How strongly the hatred of life should be taken is disputed. John Gill will not read it simply, since life is the gift of God and a blessing so dear that a man will give all he has for it; he takes the words comparatively, of a lessened regard for life beside the lovingkindness of God, which is better than life, though he reports that others think Solomon was genuinely weary of it, impatient as Job and Jonah were. John Wesley says without qualification that his life was a burden to him, and that the consideration of human designs increased his discontent. Adam Clarke reads the plural noun as the lives — of the wise man, the mad man and the fool alike, and equally the stages of a life, the child, the man and the sage — with nothing in any of them worth re-living. Keil and Delitzsch spend the verse on a smaller point, rejecting the ancient renderings that make the work a woeful burden lying upon him in favour of the idiom that makes it evil in his eyes, something that appeared evil to him; Charles Ellicott corrects the tense to the past.

The reason for the hatred is the heir, and whether a particular heir is meant divides the voices sharply. Gill reports the suspicion that Solomon is hinting at Rehoboam, and adds that it proved true; Wesley notes the same opinion without endorsing it; Clarke states it as fact and turns it into a reproach, that the wisest of men made the worst use of his wisdom, kept a thousand wives and concubines, and left one son to inherit throne and estates who was the silliest of fools. Ellicott denies any special reference, finding here only the general principle that the wisest must leave what his labour gained to another who may be destitute of wisdom; and he shifts the grievance, which he says is not so much the hardship of leaving as the injustice that the wise man should have no advantage over the fool who enjoys the same without any merit. Delitzsch draws a different conclusion from the same indefiniteness: a reigning king would not speak so coldly and vaguely of his own son and successor, so the fiction discovers itself here and the speaker is stripped of historical individuality. Gill preserves a further reading, that the labour hated is the writing of books, and that Aben Ezra applied it to the labour of this book itself. Clarke gives three plain reasons for the hatred: the labour did not answer the end it was undertaken for, its fruits can be enjoyed only a short time, and it must be left to a man who may be wise, or a knave, or a fool.
20:
The despair is a deliberate act rather than a collapse. John Gill has Solomon turning about — dropping his studies, desisting from toilsome works, settling at nothing, to relax his mind. Keil and Delitzsch make the point from the verb, which unlike its near neighbour means not a clear turning round but a turning away toward something new. Adam Clarke adds that there is no remedy: these evils cannot be prevented. The case is then stated generally: a man labours with wisdom, knowledge and what our version calls equity, and must leave it to one who never laboured for it. Charles Ellicott corrects the third word to skill or success, a noun peculiar to this book; Delitzsch agrees it is not manliness, as the Greek took it, but aptness and attendant good fortune. Clarke thinks the man is Solomon and the heir Rehoboam; John Wesley makes the injustice the point, that what prudence gained falls to one who spent his days in sloth. Gill preserves a Midrashic reading taking the labourer to be God.

The two verses that follow answer their own question negatively; Delitzsch says so flatly: nothing comes of a man's labour but disagreeableness. Gill spreads the sorrows over all a man's days from youth upward, not old age only. Clarke pictures a life whose heart is not filled with the peace of God — all its days sorrows, all its nights restless, its portion embittered by the toil of getting and disappointment in using. Wesley locates the sleeplessness in perplexing cares.

The turn to eating and drinking rests on a disputed text. Ellicott points out that the word than stands in italics in our version, so the Hebrew as it lies reads not good, interpreters generally supplying it from later passages. He gives both results without deciding: emended, the only good a man gets from his labour is the present pleasure he can make it yield, and whether he enjoys even that depends on God; unemended, the verse says it is not good for a man to eat, since this too depends on God. Delitzsch reports that the Greek translators and Jerome had a different text, yielding the contrary of what the book means. Gill records the same alternatives, including a rabbinic reading turning the clause into a question, and insists that what is commended is not the eating of the epicure but a cheerful and thankful use of what God gives. Clarke turns the counsel into verse: drive off anxious care, let reason curb the passions, enjoy the little the world affords, and look up to the giver of the power to use it aright.

The next verse turns on a single word. Our version reads more than I, making Solomon the man best placed to answer, and Wesley defends it on that ground. Gill keeps the received text too. Against them, Clarke reports eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, with the Greek, Syriac and Arabic, reading without Him; he believes this the true reading, and shows that it alone binds the surrounding sentences into one argument. Ellicott agrees it has every appearance of being right, and Delitzsch, allowing the traditional text defensible, adopts the same sense and rejects a rendering that would have the king claim an unparalleled capacity for enjoyment, a boast standing out of connection with all around it. Gill takes the closing verse as a description of the good man, none being naturally so but only such as grace makes good. Clarke reads the three gifts as knowledge of God, discernment of his hand, and a joy giving a hundred days of ease for one of pain; Wesley has the sinner given up to insatiable desire, leaving his heap to those he least desired. Delitzsch explains the final verdict as vain because purpose and issue lie far apart, and wind because what is striven for vanishes when it seems grasped.
